{{Short description|British chemist and crystallographer}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Philip George Owston'''<ref name = "Ouston">{{cite book|last = Ouston|first = Roger J.|title = A Directory of Ouston and Owston Families|publisher = Roger J. Ouston|year = 2003|chapter = Entries 1769-1771}}</ref> (January 1921 &ndash; September 2001) was a British [[chemist]] and [[X-ray crystallography|crystallographer]] for whom the [[Owston Islands]] ({{Coord|66|22|59|S|66|6|0|W|}})<ref>{{cite web|title = Place-Name Listing|publisher = [[United Kingdom Antarctic Place-Names Committee]]|url = http://www.add.scar.org:8080/geoserver/namelist.jsp|accessdate = January 9, 2011|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080507193908/http://www.add.scar.org:8080/geoserver/namelist.jsp|archivedate = May 7, 2008}}</ref> in [[Antarctica]] are named.<ref name = "NG-IA">{{cite web|url = http://www.geographic.org/geographic_names/antname.php?uni=11249&fid=antgeo_117|title = Owston Islands: Antarctica|author = National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency|author-link = National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency|publisher = Geographical Names (geographic.org)|accessdate = January 9, 2011}}</ref>    Owston was born in [[Saltburn-by-the-Sea]], [[Yorkshire]], England during January 1921 as the son of Edward Owston and Margaret Smith. He died in [[Watford]], [[Hertfordshire]], England in September 2001.<ref name = "Ouston" />

[[File:Zeise's-salt-anion-from-xtal-3D-SF.png|thumb|right|[[Space-filling model]] of [(η<sup>2</sup>-C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)PtCl<sub>3</sub>]<sup>&minus;</sup>, the [[anion]] of Zeise's salt, based on X-ray crystallographic data<ref name = "Zeise anion 1">{{cite journal|title = The crystal and molecular structure of Zeise's salt, KPtCl<sub>3</sub>.C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O|last1 = Black|first1 = M|last2 = Mais|first2 = R. H. B.|last3 = Owston|first3 = P. G.|authorlink3 = P. G. Owston|year = 1969|journal = [[Acta Crystallogr. B]]|volume = 25|issue = 9|pages = 1753–1759|doi = 10.1107/S0567740869004699| bibcode=1969AcCrB..25.1753B }}</ref><ref name = "Zeise anion 2">{{cite journal|title = A Re-determination of the Crystal and Molecular Structure of Zeise's salt, KPtCl<sub>3</sub>.C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O|last1 = Jarvis|first1 = J. A. J.|last2 = Kilbourn|first2 = B. T.|last3 = Owston|first3 = P. G.|authorlink3 = P. G. Owston|journal = [[Acta Crystallographica B|Acta Crystallogr. B]]|volume = 27|issue = 2|year = 1971|pages = 366&ndash;372|doi = 10.1107/S0567740871002231|doi-access = | bibcode=1971AcCrB..27..366J }}</ref>]]
Owston's crystallography work included the determination of the structure of [[Zeise's salt]],<ref name = "Zeise anion 1" /><ref name = "Zeise anion 2" /> the anion of which is shown at right.  Zeise's salt, {{nowrap|K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(η<sup>2</sup>-C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)]·H<sub>2</sub>O,}} was reported in 1831<ref>{{cite journal|last = Zeise|first = W. C.|author-link = William Christopher Zeise|title = Von der Wirkung zwischen Platinchlorid und Alkohol, und von den dabei entstehenden neuen Substanzen|journal = [[Annalen der Physik]]|volume = 97|issue = 4|pages = 497&ndash;541|year = 1831|doi = 10.1002/andp.18310970402|bibcode = 1831AnP....97..497Z|url = https://zenodo.org/record/1423546|language = German}}</ref> and was one of the first [[organometallic compound]]s ever discovered. However, the nature of the [[platinum]] to [[ethylene]] bond in the compound was not understood until the development of the [[Dewar–Chatt–Duncanson model]] in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite journal|title = A Historical Perspective on Dewar's Landmark Contribution to Organometallic Chemistry|last = Mingos|first = D. Michael P.|author-link = Michael Mingos|journal = [[J. Organomet. Chem.]]|year = 2001|volume = 635|issue = 1&ndash;2|pages = 1&ndash;8|doi = 10.1016/S0022-328X(01)01155-X}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title = Modern Coordination Chemistry: The Legacy of Joseph Chatt|editor1-last = Leigh|editor1-first = G. J.|editor2-last = Winterton|editor2-first = N.|year = 2002|publisher = [[RSC Publishing]]|chapter = Some Notes on the Early Development of Models of Bonding in Olefin-Metal Complexes|last = Winterton|first = N.|pages = 103&ndash;110|isbn = 978-0-85404-469-6|chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=VoBxtPb5zCcC&pg=PA103}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title = Organometallic Chemistry and Catalysis|last = Astruc|first = Didier|author-link = Didier Astruc|year = 2007|publisher = [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|pages = 41&ndash;43|isbn = 978-3-540-46128-9|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=aVyfo52-nRsC&pg=PA41}}</ref>  The [[space-filling model]] from the Owston crystal structure clearly shows that it is an organometallic species as there is direct bonding between the platinum metal centre (in blue) and the two carbon atoms of the ethylene [[ligand]] (in black).

In 1964, Owston wrote an article in ''[[New Scientist]]''<ref>{{cite journal|title = Electron Spin Resonance|volume = 24|issue = 416|date = November 5, 1964|pages = 373&ndash;377|journal = [[New Scientist]]|last = Owston|first = P. G.|author-link = P. G. Owston|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=lA9dMmYkYIsC&pg=PA392}}</ref> on the use of [[electron spin resonance]] spectroscopy in chemistry.
